{{short description|Japanese general (1849–1912)}} {{about|the general|other uses|Nogi (disambiguation)}} {{family name hatnote|Nogi|lang=Japanese}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2020}} {{Infobox officeholder | honorific_prefix = [[Kazoku|Count]] | name = Nogi Maresuke | image = Maresuke Nogi 2.jpg | image_size = | caption = Nogi standing before his house in Nogizaka, Tokyo, shortly before his suicide in 1912 | office = [[:en:Governor-General of Taiwan|Governor General of Taiwan]] | monarch = Meiji | term_start = 14 October 1896 | term_end = 26 February 1898 | predecessor = [[:en:Katsura Tarō|Katsura Tarō]] | successor = [[:en:Kodama Gentarō|Kodama Gentarō]] | nickname = Kiten
Count Nogi | birth_date = {{Birth date|1849|12|25}} | birth_place = [[:en:Edo, Japan|Edo, Japan]] | death_date = {{Death date and age|1912|09|13|1849|12|25}} | death_place = [[Tokyo]], Japan | placeofburial = | allegiance = {{flag|Empire of Japan}} | branch = {{army|Empire of Japan}} | serviceyears = 1871–1908 | Rank = [[File:帝國陸軍の階級―肩章―大将.svg|50px]] [[Four-star Rank|General]] | unit = | commands = | battles = {{tree list}} * [[Satsuma Rebellion]] * [[:en:First Sino-Japanese War|First Sino-Japanese War]] * [[Russo-Japanese War]] ** [[Siege of Port Arthur]] {{tree list/end}} | awards = {{Plainlist| * Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Rising Sun|Order of the Rising Sun]] with Paulownia Flowers * Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Golden Kite|Order of the Golden Kite]] * Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Sacred Treasure|Order of the Sacred Treasure]] * Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the [[:en:Order of the Bath|Order of the Bath]] (UK) * Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the [[Royal Victorian Order]] (UK)}} | relations = | laterwork = | native_name = {{nobold|乃木 希典}} | native_name_lang = ja | honorific_suffix = [[Senior Second Rank]] }} [[:en:Count|Count]] {{nihongo|'''Nogi Maresuke''' |乃木 希典|}}, also known as '''Kiten, Count Nogi''' [[:en:Grand Cross of the Order of the Bath|GCB]] (December 25, 1849{{spnd}}September 13, 1912), was a Japanese [[:en:General|General]] in the [[:en:Imperial Japanese Army|Imperial Japanese Army]] and a [[:en:Governor-General of Taiwan|governor-general of Taiwan]]. He was one of the commanders during the [[:en:Battle of Lushunkou|1894 capture of Port Arthur from China]] and a prominent figure in the [[Russo-Japanese War]] of 1904–05, as commander of the forces [[Siege of Port Arthur|which captured Port Arthur]] from the Russians. He was a national hero in Imperial Japan as a model of feudal loyalty and self-sacrifice, ultimately to the point of suicide. In the [[Satsuma Rebellion]], he lost a banner of the emperor in battle, for which he tried to atone with suicidal bravery in order to recapture it, until ordered to stop. In the [[Russo-Japanese War]], he captured Port Arthur but he felt that he had lost too many of his soldiers, so requested permission to commit suicide, which the emperor refused. These two events, as well as his desire not to outlive his master, motivated his suicide on the day of the funeral of the [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]. His example brought attention to the concept of ''[[:en:Bushido|Bushido]]'' and the controversial samurai practice of ''[[:en:Junshi|Junshi]]'' (following the lord in death).[[Oleg Benesch|Benesch, Oleg]]. (2014). ''Inventing the Way of the Samurai'', p. 153. == Early life == '''Nogi Nakito''' was born on December 25, 1849, at the [[:en:Chofu Domain|Chōfu Domain]] Mansion in [[:en:Edo|Edo]] (present-day [[Roppongi]], [[Tokyo]]), the third son of [[samurai]] cavalry officer (''umamawari'') Nogi Maretsugu and his wife Hisako. His father served the [[:en:Chofu Domain|Chōfu Domain]], a subsidiary domain of the [[:en:Chōshū Domain|Chōshū Domain]], and held land worth 80 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]''. His childhood name was Nakito (無人),{{Cite book |last=Ōhama |first=Tetsuya |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/744210173 |title=Nogi maresuke |date=2010 |publisher=Kōdansha |isbn=978-4-06-292028-5 |pages=19 |oclc=744210173}} literally "no one", to prevent evil spirits from coming to harm him. He was briefly known as Bunzō, after which he was renamed Maresuke. As he claimed descent from the [[:en:Izumo Province|Izumo]] [[Minamoto clan]] through the [[Sasaki clan]], he often used the name Minamoto no Maresuke in his signatures.{{Cite book |last1=Sasaki |first1=Hideaki |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/61402590 |title=Nogi Maresuke : yo wa shokun no shitei o koroshitari |last2=佐々木英昭 |date=2005 |publisher=Mineruva Shobō |isbn=4-623-04406-8 |edition=Shohan |pages=40, 113 |oclc=61402590}} == Early military career == In November 1869, by the order of the [[Nagato province|Nagato]] domain's lord, he enlisted in ''Fushimi Goshin Heisha'' ({{literal|the Fushimi Loyal Guard Barrack}}) to be trained in the French style for the domanial Army. After completing the training, he was reassigned to the Kawatō Barrack in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] as an instructor, and then as Toyōra domain's Army trainer in charge of coastal defense troops. In 1871, Nogi was commissioned as a [[Major (Rank)|major]] in the fledgling [[:en:Imperial Japanese Army|Imperial Japanese Army]]. Around this time, he renamed himself ''Maresuke'' taking a ''[[:en:Kanji|Kanji]]'' from the name of his father. In 1875, he became the 14th Infantry Regiment's attaché. The next year (1876), Nogi was named as the [[:en:Kumamoto|Kumamoto]] regional troop's Staff Officer, and transferred to command the 1st Infantry Regiment, and for his service in the [[Satsuma Rebellion]], against the forces of [[Saigō Takamori]] in [[Kyushu|Kyūshū]], he was promoted to [[:en:lieutenant colonel|lieutenant colonel]] on April 22, 1877. In a fierce battle at that time, he lost the 14th Infantry Regiment's regimental banner, which was considered to be the property of the Emperor, to the enemy. Its loss was an extreme disgrace. Nogi considered this such a grave mistake that he listed it as one of the reasons for his later suicide.Bix, Herbert. (2000). ''Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan,'' p. 42. On August 27, 1876, Nogi married Shizuko, the fourth daughter of [[Satsuma han|Satsuma]] ''samurai'' Yuji Sadano, who was then 20 years old. As Nogi was 28 years old, it was a very late marriage for that time, considering that the average age to marry was in the early 20s. On August 28, 1877, their first son Katsunori was born, and Nogi bought his first house at Niizakamachi, [[:en:Akasaka, Tokyo|Akasaka, Tokyo]]. In 1879, his second son Yasunori was born.{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}} He was promoted to [[:en:Colonel|Colonel]] on April 29, 1880. He was posted to Nagoya during the early Meiji era. The warehouse in the Sannomaru enceinte of [[Nagoya Castle]] was probably constructed in 1880 (Meiji 13) as an army ammunition depot. It was named later after him.{{cite web | url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/113094 | title=乃木倉庫 文化遺産オンライン }} Promoted [[:en:major general|major general]] on May 21, 1885, in 1887 Nogi went to [[:en:Germany|Germany]] with [[:en:Kawakami Soroku|Kawakami Soroku]] to study European [[:en:Military strategy|Military strategy]] and tactics.National Diet Library: "Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures," [http://www.ndl.go.jp/portrait/e/datas/160.html?c=7 Nogi Maresuke.] In 1894, during the [[:en:First Sino-Japanese War|First Sino-Japanese War]], Major-General Nogi commanded the First Infantry Brigade which penetrated the Chinese defenses and successfully occupied [[:en:Lüshunkou|Port Arthur]] in only one day of combat. As such, he was a senior commander during the [[:en:Port Arthur massacre (China)|Port Arthur massacre]]. The following year, he was promoted to [[:en:lieutenant general|lieutenant general]] (April 29, 1895) and assigned to the [[:en:2nd Division (Imperial Japanese Army)|Second Division]], tasked with the [[:en:Japanese invasion of Taiwan (1895)|invasion of Taiwan]]. Nogi remained with the occupation forces in Taiwan until 1898. In 1899, he was recalled to Japan, and placed in command of the newly formed 11th Infantry Brigade, based in [[:en:Kagawa Prefecture|Kagawa]].{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}}{{Cite book|title=500 Great Military Leaders|last=Tucker|first=Spencer C.|publisher=ABC-CLIO|date=December 16, 2014|isbn=978-1598847574|pages=560}} == Political career == After the war, he was elevated to ''danshaku'' ([[:en:Baron|Baron]]); and he was conferred with the [[:en:Order of the Golden Kite|Order of the Golden Kite]], 1st class.[https://books.google.com/books?id=x70UAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA1139&dq= "Nogi, Maresuke,"] ''Encyclopædia Britannica'' (12th ed.), Vol. XXX, p. 1139. Nogi was appointed as the third Japanese [[:en:Governor-General of Taiwan|Governor-General of Taiwan]] from October 14, 1896, to February 1898. When moving to Taiwan, he moved his entire family, and during their time in Taiwan, his mother contracted [[:en:Malaria|Malaria]] and died. This led Nogi to take measures to improve on the health care infrastructure of the island. However, unlike many of his contemporaries as officers, Nogi expressed no interest in pursuing politics.{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}} == Russo-Japanese War == [[File:Fronte (15).jpg|thumb|right|Nogi standing in the center facing a captured Russian gun crew outside [[:en:Port Arthur naval base|Port Arthur]] on January 2, 1905]] In 1904, Nogi was recalled to active service on the occasion of the [[Russo-Japanese War]], and was promoted to army [[:en:General|General]] in command of the [[:en:Japanese Third Army|Japanese Third Army]], with an initial strength of approximately 90,000 men and assigned to the capture of the [[Russia]]n-held [[:en:Lüshunkou|Port Arthur]] on the southern tip of [[:en:en:Liaodong Peninsula|en:Liaodong Peninsula]], [[:en:Manchuria|Manchuria]]. Nogi's forces landed shortly after the [[:en:Battle of Nanshan|Battle of Nanshan]], in which his eldest son, serving with the [[:en:Japanese Second Army|Japanese Second Army]], was killed.Connaughton, Richard. (1988). ''Rising Sun and Tumbling Bear'', p. 101. Advancing slowly down the Liaodong Peninsula, Nogi encountered unexpectedly strong resistance, and far more fortifications than he had experienced ten years earlier against the Chinese. [[Image:Nogi and Stessel.jpg|thumb|left|Nogi is seated in the center next to Russian general [[:en:Anatoly Stessel|Anatoly Stessel]] after Russian forces surrendered at Port Arthur on January 2, 1905.]] The attack against Port Arthur quickly turned into the lengthy [[Siege of Port Arthur]], an engagement lasting from August 1, 1904, to January 2, 1905, costing the Japanese massive losses. Due to the mounting casualties and failure of Nogi to overcome Port Arthur's defenses, there was mounting pressure within the Japanese government and military to relieve him of command. However, in an unprecedented action, [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] spoke out during the [[Supreme War Council (Japan)]] meeting, defending Nogi and demanding that he be kept in command.{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}} After the fall of Port Arthur, Nogi was regarded as a national hero. He led his Third Army against the Russian forces at the final [[:en:Battle of Mukden|Battle of Mukden]], ending the land combat phase of operations of the war.Jukes, Geoffrey. (2002). ''The Russo-Japanese War 1904–1905'', p. 66. British historian [[Richard Storry]] noted that Nogi imposed the best of the Japanese ''samurai'' tradition on the men under his command such that "...the conduct of the Japanese during the Russo-Japanese War towards both prisoners and Chinese civilians won the respect, and indeed admiration, of the world".[[Richard Storry|Storry, Richard]]. (1960). ''A History of Modern Japan'', p. 217. Both of Nogi's sons, who were army lieutenants during the war, were killed in action. Though Nogi's elder son Katsunori (August 28, 1879 – May 27, 1904) had been a sickly child, he had managed to enter the imperial military academy on his third try. He was hit in the abdomen at the Battle of Nanshan and died of blood loss while undergoing surgery at a field hospital. His second son Yasunori (December 16, 1881 – November 30, 1904), a second lieutenant at Port Arthur, fell on a rocky slope, striking his head and dying instantly. Yasunori received a posthumous promotion to lieutenant, and was buried by his father in the Aoyama cemetery. At the end of the war, Nogi made a report directly to Emperor Meiji during a ''[[:en:Gozen Kaigi|Gozen Kaigi]]''. When explaining battles of the Siege of Port Arthur in detail, he broke down and wept, apologizing for the 56,000 lives lost in that campaign and asking to be allowed to kill himself in atonement. Emperor Meiji told him that suicide was unacceptable, as all responsibility for the war was due to imperial orders, and that Nogi must remain alive, at least as long as he himself lived.Keene, Donald. (2005). '' Emperor of Japan, Meiji and his World'', pp. 712–713. == Postwar career == After the war, Nogi was elevated to the title of [[:en:Count|Count]] and awarded the [[:en:Order of the Rising Sun|Order of the Rising Sun with Paulownia Flowers, Grand Cordon]], 1907. As head of the [[:en:Gakushuin|Peers' School]] from 1908 to 1912, he was the mentor of the young [[:en:Hirohito|Hirohito]], and was, perhaps, the most important influence on the life of the future emperor of Japan.Bix, Herbert. (2000). ''Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan,'' pp. 36-37, 43. Nogi spent most of his personal fortune on hospitals for wounded soldiers and on memorial monuments erected around the country in commemoration of those killed during the Russo-Japanese War. He also successfully petitioned the Japanese government to erect a Russian-style memorial monument in Port Arthur to the Russian dead of that campaign.{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}} == Scouting == Nogi is significant to [[Scout Association of Japan|Scouting in Japan]], as in 1911, he went to England in attendance on [[:en:Prince Higashifushimi Yorihito|Prince Higashifushimi Yorihito]] for the [[:en:Coronation of George V and Mary|coronation of King George V]]. The General, as the "Defender of Port Arthur" was introduced to [[Robert Baden-Powell, 1st Baron Baden-Powell|General Robert Baden-Powell]], the "Defender of [[Siege of Mafeking|Mafeking]]", by [[:en:Herbert Kitchener, 1st Earl Kitchener|Lord Kitchener]], whose expression "Once a Scout, always a Scout" remains to this day. == Suicide == [[File:Room in which Nogi committed suicide with his wife.JPG|thumb|upright|Room in which Nogi Maresuke committed suicide with his wife]] Nogi and his wife Shizuko committed suicide by ''[[seppuku]]'' shortly after the [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]'s funeral cortege left the palace.Noss, John Boyer. (1980). ''Man's Religions'', p. 319. The ritual suicide was in accordance with the ''samurai'' practice of following one's master to death (''[[:en:Junshi|Junshi]]'').Lyell, Thomas. (1948). ''Case History of Japan,'' p. 142. In his [[suicide letter]], he said that he wished to expiate for his disgrace in Kyūshū, and for the thousands of casualties at Port Arthur. He also donated his body to medical science.[[Image:House of Maresuke Nogi.jpg|thumb|left|House of Maresuke Nogi in [[Nogizaka]]]]All four members of the Nogi family are buried at [[:en:Aoyama Cemetery|Aoyama Cemetery]] in Tokyo. Under [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], Nogi was revered as a ''[[kami]]''. [[Nogi Shrine (Tokyo)|Nogi Shrine]], a [[Shinto shrine]] in his honor, still exists on the site of his house in [[:en:Minato, Tokyo|Nogizaka]], Tokyo. His memory is also honored in other locations such as the [[Nogi Shrine (Kyoto)|Nogi Shrine]] in [[Fushimi-ku, Kyoto#Sights|Fushimi-ku]], Kyoto, where the mausoleum of Emperor Meiji was established.[http://www.geocities.jp/kyo_nogi/ Nogi Jinja] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121022151620/http://www.geocities.jp/kyo_nogi/ |date=October 22, 2012 }}, Kyoto. == Legacy == [[File:Nogi-jinja (Minato, Tokyo).jpg|thumb|Nogi Shrine in Nogizaka]] [[Image:Ziziphus jujuba.jpg|thumb|right|150px|The [[Ziziphus jujuba]] which written in ''[[:en:Monbusho|Monbusho]]'' chant lyrics, located in Nogi's mansion]] Nogi's ''seppuku'' immediately created a sensation and a controversy. Some writers claimed that it reflected Nogi's disgust with the profligacy and decline in moral values of late Meiji Japan. Others pointed to Nogi's own suicide note, calling it an act of atonement for mistakes in his military career. In either case, Nogi's suicide marked the end of an era, and it had a profound impact on contemporary writers, such as [[:en:Mori Ōgai|Mori Ōgai]], [[:en:Kuroiwa Shūroku|Kuroiwa Ruikō]] and [[:en:Natsume Sōseki|Natsume Sōseki]]. For the public, Nogi became a symbol of loyalty and sacrifice. The epic historical novel ''[[:en:Saka no Ue no Kumo|Saka no Ue no Kumo]]'' portrays Nogi as floundering at the [[Siege of Port Arthur]] and having to be relieved by [[:en:Kodama Gentarō|Kodama Gentarō]]. Several books have been released in recent years rehabilitating Nogi's image and showing he was a competent leader. [[File:Nagoya cstl nogi soko.jpg|thumb|left|Nogi Warehouse at [[Nagoya Castle]]]] The Nogi Warehouse in the Sannomaru enceinte of Nagoya Castle was named after him.{{cite web | url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/113094 | title=乃木倉庫 文化遺産オンライン }} ==Man of letters== Nogi is also noted in Japan as a man of letters. His [[:en:Kanshi (poetry)|Kanshi]] poems ([[:en:Chinese poetry|poems in the Chinese language]]) were especially popular among the Japanese during his time. Three of his Kanshi poems are famous.[http://www.nogijinja.or.jp/shahou/main.html Gen. Nogi's Relics at Nogi Shrine] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120225022226/http://www.nogijinja.or.jp/shahou/main.html |date=February 25, 2012 }} (in Japanese) Right after the [[:en:Battle of Nanshan|Battle of Nanshan]] of 1904, in which he lost his eldest son, he wrote: {| class="wikitable" style="margin:auto" |- !　金州城外の作 ! Written Outside the Walls of [[:en:Jinzhou District|Jinzhou]] |- | align=left | 山川草木轉荒涼
十里風腥新戰場
征馬不前人不語
金州城外立斜陽 | align=left | Mountains and rivers, trees and grass, have become cold and desolate.
For ten ''[[:en:Li (unit)|li]]'', the foul odor of blood drifts on the wind over new battlefields.
My brave horse would not advance, and the soldiers are silent.
I stand outside Jinzhou Town, in the setting sun. |} After the battle of [[:en:Hill 203|Hill 203]] of 1904–05, in which he lost his second son, he wrote: {| class="wikitable" style="margin:auto" |- ! 爾靈山 ! Nireisan |- | align=left | 爾靈山嶮豈難攀
男子功名期克艱
鐵血覆山山形改
萬人齊仰爾靈山 | align=left | Nireisan was indeed difficult to climb,
But it was overcome by the deeds of young men.
Under a mantle of iron and blood, the mountain's shape is changed.
Now all look up in awe at Nireisan. |} After the end of the [[Russo-Japanese War]], he wrote: {| class="wikitable" style="margin:auto" |- ! 凱旋 ! Triumphant Return |- | align=left | 皇師百萬征強虜
野戰攻城屍作山
愧我何顔看父老
凱歌今日幾人還 | align=left | The Emperor's army, a million strong, set out to punish the powerful savages of the north.
On the battlefield, in the midst of the sieges, the bodies of the dead piled up like mountains.
I am ashamed to show my face to the fathers who remain back home,
though we few return today in triumph. |} == Honors == [[Image:Maresuke Nogi stamp.jpg|thumb|145px|An [[:en:Empire of Japan|Imperial Japanese]] stamp from 1938 depicting Nogi]] ===Peerages=== * 1895: Baron (August 20) * 1907: Count (September 21) ===Decorations=== * 1897: Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Sacred Treasure|Order of the Sacred Treasure]] (June 26; Second Class: April 29, 1894) * 1906: Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Golden Kite|Order of the Golden Kite]] (April 1) (Third Class: August 20, 1895) * 1906: [[:en:Order of the Rising Sun|Grand Cordon of the Order of the Rising Sun with Paulownia Flowers]] (April 1). (Second Class: August 20, 1895; Third Class: April 7, 1885) * 1905: [[:en:Pour le Mérite|Pour le Mérite]] (January 10) * 1907: Grand Cross of the [[:en:Legion of Honour|Legion of Honour]] (April 16) * 1909: Chilean Gold Medal of Merit (April 28) * 1911: Grand Cross of the Order of the Star of Romania (October 25) * 1911: Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the [[Royal Victorian Order|Knights Grand Cross of the Royal Victorian Order]] (GCVO) * 1911: Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the [[:en:Order of the Bath|Order of the Bath]], Military Division (UK) (GCB) (January 1).[http://www.london-gazette.co.uk/about London Gazette:] [http://www.london-gazette.co.uk/issues/28567/supplements/1 Issue No. 28567, p. 1 (29 December 1911).] ===Court order of precedence=== * 1871: Senior seventh Rank (December) * 1873: Sixth Rank (June 25) * 1879: Senior sixth Rank (December 20) * 1880: Fifth Rank (June 8) * 1885: Senior fifth Rank (July 25) * 1893: Senior fourth Rank (April 11) * 1896: Third Rank (December 21) * 1904: Senior third Rank (June 6) * 1909: Second Rank (July 10) * 1916: Senior second Rank (posthumous) ==Portrayals== Maresuke was portrayed by [[Tatsuya Nakadai]] in the 1980 Japanese [[:en:War film|war]] [[:en:Drama (film and television)|drama film]] ''[[The Battle of Port Arthur]]'' (sometimes referred as ''203 Kochi'').[https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0080316/ ''The Battle of Port Arthur'' (''203 Koshi'')] in the [[:en:Internet Movie Database|Internet Movie Database]] Directed by [[Toshio Masuda (director)|Toshio Masuda]] the film depicted the [[Siege of Port Arthur]] during the [[Russo-Japanese War]] and starred Nakadai as General Maresuke, [[Tetsurō Tamba]] as General [[:en:Kodama Gentarō|Kodama Gentarō]], and [[Toshiro Mifune|Toshirō Mifune]] as [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]. In the [[:en:NHK|NHK]] television adaptation of [[Ryōtarō Shiba]]'s epic [[:en:Saka no Ue no Kumo (TV series)|''Saka no Ue no Kumo'']], which aired from 2009 to 2011, Nogi was portrayed by actor [[:en:Akira Emoto|Akira Emoto]]. In the manga and [[:en:NHK|NHK]] television adaptation of ''[[:en:Monster (manga)|Monster]]'', General Nogi is mentioned by the Turkish elder and community leader, Mr. Deniz, convincing the others to trust Dr. Kenzo Tenma and a local prostitute when they attempt to convince the leaders of FRankfurt's Turkish Quarter to be wary of an imminent arson attack by neo-Nazis, led by The Baby. Deniz makes reference to an incident wherein General Nogi saved an Ottoman fleet of the Turkish Navy that had run aground in the Pacific. Although this is most likely a confusion with [[Yamada Torajirō]] who did assist after the sinking of [[:en:Ottoman frigate Ertuğrul#Shipwreck|Ottoman frigate Ertuğrul#Shipwreck]]. == Notes == {{reflist}} == References == {{refbegin}} * [[:en:Herbert Bix|Bix]], Herbert P. {{short description|Japanese general (1849–1912)}} {{about|the general|other uses|Nogi (disambiguation)}} {{family name hatnote|Nogi|lang=Japanese}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2020}} {{Infobox officeholder | honorific_prefix = [[Kazoku|Count]] | name = Nogi Maresuke | image = Maresuke Nogi 2.jpg | image_size = | caption = Nogi standing before his house in Nogizaka, Tokyo, shortly before his suicide in 1912 | office = [[:en:Governor-General of Taiwan|Governor General of Taiwan]] | monarch = Meiji | term_start = 14 October 1896 | term_end = 26 February 1898 | predecessor = [[:en:Katsura Tarō|Katsura Tarō]] | successor = [[:en:Kodama Gentarō|Kodama Gentarō]] | nickname = Kiten
Count Nogi | birth_date = {{Birth date|1849|12|25}} | birth_place = [[:en:Edo, Japan|Edo, Japan]] | death_date = {{Death date and age|1912|09|13|1849|12|25}} | death_place = [[Tokyo]], Japan | placeofburial = | allegiance = {{flag|Empire of Japan}} | branch = {{army|Empire of Japan}} | serviceyears = 1871–1908 | Rank = [[File:帝國陸軍の階級―肩章―大将.svg|50px]] [[Four-star Rank|General]] | unit = | commands = | battles = {{tree list}} * [[Satsuma Rebellion]] * [[:en:First Sino-Japanese War|First Sino-Japanese War]] * [[Russo-Japanese War]] ** [[Siege of Port Arthur]] {{tree list/end}} | awards = {{Plainlist| * Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Rising Sun|Order of the Rising Sun]] with Paulownia Flowers * Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Golden Kite|Order of the Golden Kite]] * Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Sacred Treasure|Order of the Sacred Treasure]] * Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the [[:en:Order of the Bath|Order of the Bath]] (UK) * Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the [[Royal Victorian Order]] (UK)}} | relations = | laterwork = | native_name = {{nobold|乃木 希典}} | native_name_lang = ja | honorific_suffix = [[Senior Second Rank]] }} [[:en:Count|Count]] {{nihongo|'''Nogi Maresuke''' |乃木 希典|}}, also known as '''Kiten, Count Nogi''' [[:en:Grand Cross of the Order of the Bath|GCB]] (December 25, 1849{{spnd}}September 13, 1912), was a Japanese [[:en:General|General]] in the [[:en:Imperial Japanese Army|Imperial Japanese Army]] and a [[:en:Governor-General of Taiwan|governor-general of Taiwan]]. He was one of the commanders during the [[:en:Battle of Lushunkou|1894 capture of Port Arthur from China]] and a prominent figure in the [[Russo-Japanese War]] of 1904–05, as commander of the forces [[Siege of Port Arthur|which captured Port Arthur]] from the Russians. He was a national hero in Imperial Japan as a model of feudal loyalty and self-sacrifice, ultimately to the point of suicide. In the [[Satsuma Rebellion]], he lost a banner of the emperor in battle, for which he tried to atone with suicidal bravery in order to recapture it, until ordered to stop. In the [[Russo-Japanese War]], he captured Port Arthur but he felt that he had lost too many of his soldiers, so requested permission to commit suicide, which the emperor refused. These two events, as well as his desire not to outlive his master, motivated his suicide on the day of the funeral of the [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]. His example brought attention to the concept of ''[[:en:Bushido|Bushido]]'' and the controversial samurai practice of ''[[:en:Junshi|Junshi]]'' (following the lord in death).[[Oleg Benesch|Benesch, Oleg]]. (2014). ''Inventing the Way of the Samurai'', p. 153. == Early life == '''Nogi Nakito''' was born on December 25, 1849, at the [[:en:Chofu Domain|Chōfu Domain]] Mansion in [[:en:Edo|Edo]] (present-day [[Roppongi]], [[Tokyo]]), the third son of [[samurai]] cavalry officer (''umamawari'') Nogi Maretsugu and his wife Hisako. His father served the [[:en:Chofu Domain|Chōfu Domain]], a subsidiary domain of the [[:en:Chōshū Domain|Chōshū Domain]], and held land worth 80 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]''. His childhood name was Nakito (無人),{{Cite book |last=Ōhama |first=Tetsuya |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/744210173 |title=Nogi maresuke |date=2010 |publisher=Kōdansha |isbn=978-4-06-292028-5 |pages=19 |oclc=744210173}} literally "no one", to prevent evil spirits from coming to harm him. He was briefly known as Bunzō, after which he was renamed Maresuke. As he claimed descent from the [[:en:Izumo Province|Izumo]] [[Minamoto clan]] through the [[Sasaki clan]], he often used the name Minamoto no Maresuke in his signatures.{{Cite book |last1=Sasaki |first1=Hideaki |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/61402590 |title=Nogi Maresuke : yo wa shokun no shitei o koroshitari |last2=佐々木英昭 |date=2005 |publisher=Mineruva Shobō |isbn=4-623-04406-8 |edition=Shohan |pages=40, 113 |oclc=61402590}} == Early military career == In November 1869, by the order of the [[Nagato province|Nagato]] domain's lord, he enlisted in ''Fushimi Goshin Heisha'' ({{literal|the Fushimi Loyal Guard Barrack}}) to be trained in the French style for the domanial Army. After completing the training, he was reassigned to the Kawatō Barrack in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] as an instructor, and then as Toyōra domain's Army trainer in charge of coastal defense troops. In 1871, Nogi was commissioned as a [[Major (Rank)|major]] in the fledgling [[:en:Imperial Japanese Army|Imperial Japanese Army]]. Around this time, he renamed himself ''Maresuke'' taking a ''[[:en:Kanji|Kanji]]'' from the name of his father. In 1875, he became the 14th Infantry Regiment's attaché. The next year (1876), Nogi was named as the [[:en:Kumamoto|Kumamoto]] regional troop's Staff Officer, and transferred to command the 1st Infantry Regiment, and for his service in the [[Satsuma Rebellion]], against the forces of [[Saigō Takamori]] in [[Kyushu|Kyūshū]], he was promoted to [[:en:lieutenant colonel|lieutenant colonel]] on April 22, 1877. In a fierce battle at that time, he lost the 14th Infantry Regiment's regimental banner, which was considered to be the property of the Emperor, to the enemy. Its loss was an extreme disgrace. Nogi considered this such a grave mistake that he listed it as one of the reasons for his later suicide.Bix, Herbert. (2000). ''Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan,'' p. 42. On August 27, 1876, Nogi married Shizuko, the fourth daughter of [[Satsuma han|Satsuma]] ''samurai'' Yuji Sadano, who was then 20 years old. As Nogi was 28 years old, it was a very late marriage for that time, considering that the average age to marry was in the early 20s. On August 28, 1877, their first son Katsunori was born, and Nogi bought his first house at Niizakamachi, [[:en:Akasaka, Tokyo|Akasaka, Tokyo]]. In 1879, his second son Yasunori was born.{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}} He was promoted to [[:en:Colonel|Colonel]] on April 29, 1880. He was posted to Nagoya during the early Meiji era. The warehouse in the Sannomaru enceinte of [[Nagoya Castle]] was probably constructed in 1880 (Meiji 13) as an army ammunition depot. It was named later after him.{{cite web | url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/113094 | title=乃木倉庫 文化遺産オンライン }} Promoted [[:en:major general|major general]] on May 21, 1885, in 1887 Nogi went to [[:en:Germany|Germany]] with [[:en:Kawakami Soroku|Kawakami Soroku]] to study European [[:en:Military strategy|Military strategy]] and tactics.National Diet Library: "Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures," [http://www.ndl.go.jp/portrait/e/datas/160.html?c=7 Nogi Maresuke.] In 1894, during the [[:en:First Sino-Japanese War|First Sino-Japanese War]], Major-General Nogi commanded the First Infantry Brigade which penetrated the Chinese defenses and successfully occupied [[:en:Lüshunkou|Port Arthur]] in only one day of combat. As such, he was a senior commander during the [[:en:Port Arthur massacre (China)|Port Arthur massacre]]. The following year, he was promoted to [[:en:lieutenant general|lieutenant general]] (April 29, 1895) and assigned to the [[:en:2nd Division (Imperial Japanese Army)|Second Division]], tasked with the [[:en:Japanese invasion of Taiwan (1895)|invasion of Taiwan]]. Nogi remained with the occupation forces in Taiwan until 1898. In 1899, he was recalled to Japan, and placed in command of the newly formed 11th Infantry Brigade, based in [[:en:Kagawa Prefecture|Kagawa]].{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}}{{Cite book|title=500 Great Military Leaders|last=Tucker|first=Spencer C.|publisher=ABC-CLIO|date=December 16, 2014|isbn=978-1598847574|pages=560}} == Political career == After the war, he was elevated to ''danshaku'' ([[:en:Baron|Baron]]); and he was conferred with the [[:en:Order of the Golden Kite|Order of the Golden Kite]], 1st class.[https://books.google.com/books?id=x70UAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA1139&dq= "Nogi, Maresuke,"] ''Encyclopædia Britannica'' (12th ed.), Vol. XXX, p. 1139. Nogi was appointed as the third Japanese [[:en:Governor-General of Taiwan|Governor-General of Taiwan]] from October 14, 1896, to February 1898. When moving to Taiwan, he moved his entire family, and during their time in Taiwan, his mother contracted [[:en:Malaria|Malaria]] and died. This led Nogi to take measures to improve on the health care infrastructure of the island. However, unlike many of his contemporaries as officers, Nogi expressed no interest in pursuing politics.{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}} == Russo-Japanese War == [[File:Fronte (15).jpg|thumb|right|Nogi standing in the center facing a captured Russian gun crew outside [[:en:Port Arthur naval base|Port Arthur]] on January 2, 1905]] In 1904, Nogi was recalled to active service on the occasion of the [[Russo-Japanese War]], and was promoted to army [[:en:General|General]] in command of the [[:en:Japanese Third Army|Japanese Third Army]], with an initial strength of approximately 90,000 men and assigned to the capture of the [[Russia]]n-held [[:en:Lüshunkou|Port Arthur]] on the southern tip of [[:en:en:Liaodong Peninsula|en:Liaodong Peninsula]], [[:en:Manchuria|Manchuria]]. Nogi's forces landed shortly after the [[:en:Battle of Nanshan|Battle of Nanshan]], in which his eldest son, serving with the [[:en:Japanese Second Army|Japanese Second Army]], was killed.Connaughton, Richard. (1988). ''Rising Sun and Tumbling Bear'', p. 101. Advancing slowly down the Liaodong Peninsula, Nogi encountered unexpectedly strong resistance, and far more fortifications than he had experienced ten years earlier against the Chinese. [[Image:Nogi and Stessel.jpg|thumb|left|Nogi is seated in the center next to Russian general [[:en:Anatoly Stessel|Anatoly Stessel]] after Russian forces surrendered at Port Arthur on January 2, 1905.]] The attack against Port Arthur quickly turned into the lengthy [[Siege of Port Arthur]], an engagement lasting from August 1, 1904, to January 2, 1905, costing the Japanese massive losses. Due to the mounting casualties and failure of Nogi to overcome Port Arthur's defenses, there was mounting pressure within the Japanese government and military to relieve him of command. However, in an unprecedented action, [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] spoke out during the [[Supreme War Council (Japan)]] meeting, defending Nogi and demanding that he be kept in command.{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}} After the fall of Port Arthur, Nogi was regarded as a national hero. He led his Third Army against the Russian forces at the final [[:en:Battle of Mukden|Battle of Mukden]], ending the land combat phase of operations of the war.Jukes, Geoffrey. (2002). ''The Russo-Japanese War 1904–1905'', p. 66. British historian [[Richard Storry]] noted that Nogi imposed the best of the Japanese ''samurai'' tradition on the men under his command such that "...the conduct of the Japanese during the Russo-Japanese War towards both prisoners and Chinese civilians won the respect, and indeed admiration, of the world".[[Richard Storry|Storry, Richard]]. (1960). ''A History of Modern Japan'', p. 217. Both of Nogi's sons, who were army lieutenants during the war, were killed in action. Though Nogi's elder son Katsunori (August 28, 1879 – May 27, 1904) had been a sickly child, he had managed to enter the imperial military academy on his third try. He was hit in the abdomen at the Battle of Nanshan and died of blood loss while undergoing surgery at a field hospital. His second son Yasunori (December 16, 1881 – November 30, 1904), a second lieutenant at Port Arthur, fell on a rocky slope, striking his head and dying instantly. Yasunori received a posthumous promotion to lieutenant, and was buried by his father in the Aoyama cemetery. At the end of the war, Nogi made a report directly to Emperor Meiji during a ''[[:en:Gozen Kaigi|Gozen Kaigi]]''. When explaining battles of the Siege of Port Arthur in detail, he broke down and wept, apologizing for the 56,000 lives lost in that campaign and asking to be allowed to kill himself in atonement. Emperor Meiji told him that suicide was unacceptable, as all responsibility for the war was due to imperial orders, and that Nogi must remain alive, at least as long as he himself lived.Keene, Donald. (2005). '' Emperor of Japan, Meiji and his World'', pp. 712–713. == Postwar career == After the war, Nogi was elevated to the title of [[:en:Count|Count]] and awarded the [[:en:Order of the Rising Sun|Order of the Rising Sun with Paulownia Flowers, Grand Cordon]], 1907. As head of the [[:en:Gakushuin|Peers' School]] from 1908 to 1912, he was the mentor of the young [[:en:Hirohito|Hirohito]], and was, perhaps, the most important influence on the life of the future emperor of Japan.Bix, Herbert. (2000). ''Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan,'' pp. 36-37, 43. Nogi spent most of his personal fortune on hospitals for wounded soldiers and on memorial monuments erected around the country in commemoration of those killed during the Russo-Japanese War. He also successfully petitioned the Japanese government to erect a Russian-style memorial monument in Port Arthur to the Russian dead of that campaign.{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}} == Scouting == Nogi is significant to [[Scout Association of Japan|Scouting in Japan]], as in 1911, he went to England in attendance on [[:en:Prince Higashifushimi Yorihito|Prince Higashifushimi Yorihito]] for the [[:en:Coronation of George V and Mary|coronation of King George V]]. The General, as the "Defender of Port Arthur" was introduced to [[Robert Baden-Powell, 1st Baron Baden-Powell|General Robert Baden-Powell]], the "Defender of [[Siege of Mafeking|Mafeking]]", by [[:en:Herbert Kitchener, 1st Earl Kitchener|Lord Kitchener]], whose expression "Once a Scout, always a Scout" remains to this day. == Suicide == [[File:Room in which Nogi committed suicide with his wife.JPG|thumb|upright|Room in which Nogi Maresuke committed suicide with his wife]] Nogi and his wife Shizuko committed suicide by ''[[seppuku]]'' shortly after the [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]'s funeral cortege left the palace.Noss, John Boyer. (1980). ''Man's Religions'', p. 319. The ritual suicide was in accordance with the ''samurai'' practice of following one's master to death (''[[:en:Junshi|Junshi]]'').Lyell, Thomas. (1948). ''Case History of Japan,'' p. 142. In his [[suicide letter]], he said that he wished to expiate for his disgrace in Kyūshū, and for the thousands of casualties at Port Arthur. He also donated his body to medical science.[[Image:House of Maresuke Nogi.jpg|thumb|left|House of Maresuke Nogi in [[Nogizaka]]]]All four members of the Nogi family are buried at [[:en:Aoyama Cemetery|Aoyama Cemetery]] in Tokyo. Under [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], Nogi was revered as a ''[[kami]]''. [[Nogi Shrine (Tokyo)|Nogi Shrine]], a [[Shinto shrine]] in his honor, still exists on the site of his house in [[:en:Minato, Tokyo|Nogizaka]], Tokyo. His memory is also honored in other locations such as the [[Nogi Shrine (Kyoto)|Nogi Shrine]] in [[Fushimi-ku, Kyoto#Sights|Fushimi-ku]], Kyoto, where the mausoleum of Emperor Meiji was established.[http://www.geocities.jp/kyo_nogi/ Nogi Jinja] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121022151620/http://www.geocities.jp/kyo_nogi/ |date=October 22, 2012 }}, Kyoto. == Legacy == [[File:Nogi-jinja (Minato, Tokyo).jpg|thumb|Nogi Shrine in Nogizaka]] [[Image:Ziziphus jujuba.jpg|thumb|right|150px|The [[Ziziphus jujuba]] which written in ''[[:en:Monbusho|Monbusho]]'' chant lyrics, located in Nogi's mansion]] Nogi's ''seppuku'' immediately created a sensation and a controversy. Some writers claimed that it reflected Nogi's disgust with the profligacy and decline in moral values of late Meiji Japan. Others pointed to Nogi's own suicide note, calling it an act of atonement for mistakes in his military career. In either case, Nogi's suicide marked the end of an era, and it had a profound impact on contemporary writers, such as [[:en:Mori Ōgai|Mori Ōgai]], [[:en:Kuroiwa Shūroku|Kuroiwa Ruikō]] and [[:en:Natsume Sōseki|Natsume Sōseki]]. For the public, Nogi became a symbol of loyalty and sacrifice. The epic historical novel ''[[:en:Saka no Ue no Kumo|Saka no Ue no Kumo]]'' portrays Nogi as floundering at the [[Siege of Port Arthur]] and having to be relieved by [[:en:Kodama Gentarō|Kodama Gentarō]]. Several books have been released in recent years rehabilitating Nogi's image and showing he was a competent leader. [[File:Nagoya cstl nogi soko.jpg|thumb|left|Nogi Warehouse at [[Nagoya Castle]]]] The Nogi Warehouse in the Sannomaru enceinte of Nagoya Castle was named after him.{{cite web | url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/113094 | title=乃木倉庫 文化遺産オンライン }} ==Man of letters== Nogi is also noted in Japan as a man of letters. His [[:en:Kanshi (poetry)|Kanshi]] poems ([[:en:Chinese poetry|poems in the Chinese language]]) were especially popular among the Japanese during his time. Three of his Kanshi poems are famous.[http://www.nogijinja.or.jp/shahou/main.html Gen. Nogi's Relics at Nogi Shrine] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120225022226/http://www.nogijinja.or.jp/shahou/main.html |date=February 25, 2012 }} (in Japanese) Right after the [[:en:Battle of Nanshan|Battle of Nanshan]] of 1904, in which he lost his eldest son, he wrote: {| class="wikitable" style="margin:auto" |- !　金州城外の作 ! Written Outside the Walls of [[:en:Jinzhou District|Jinzhou]] |- | align=left | 山川草木轉荒涼
十里風腥新戰場
征馬不前人不語
金州城外立斜陽 | align=left | Mountains and rivers, trees and grass, have become cold and desolate.
For ten ''[[:en:Li (unit)|li]]'', the foul odor of blood drifts on the wind over new battlefields.
My brave horse would not advance, and the soldiers are silent.
I stand outside Jinzhou Town, in the setting sun. |} After the battle of [[:en:Hill 203|Hill 203]] of 1904–05, in which he lost his second son, he wrote: {| class="wikitable" style="margin:auto" |- ! 爾靈山 ! Nireisan |- | align=left | 爾靈山嶮豈難攀
男子功名期克艱
鐵血覆山山形改
萬人齊仰爾靈山 | align=left | Nireisan was indeed difficult to climb,
But it was overcome by the deeds of young men.
Under a mantle of iron and blood, the mountain's shape is changed.
Now all look up in awe at Nireisan. |} After the end of the [[Russo-Japanese War]], he wrote: {| class="wikitable" style="margin:auto" |- ! 凱旋 ! Triumphant Return |- | align=left | 皇師百萬征強虜
野戰攻城屍作山
愧我何顔看父老
凱歌今日幾人還 | align=left | The Emperor's army, a million strong, set out to punish the powerful savages of the north.
On the battlefield, in the midst of the sieges, the bodies of the dead piled up like mountains.
I am ashamed to show my face to the fathers who remain back home,
though we few return today in triumph. |} == Honors == [[Image:Maresuke Nogi stamp.jpg|thumb|145px|An [[:en:Empire of Japan|Imperial Japanese]] stamp from 1938 depicting Nogi]] ===Peerages=== * 1895: Baron (August 20) * 1907: Count (September 21) ===Decorations=== * 1897: Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Sacred Treasure|Order of the Sacred Treasure]] (June 26; Second Class: April 29, 1894) * 1906: Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Golden Kite|Order of the Golden Kite]] (April 1) (Third Class: August 20, 1895) * 1906: [[:en:Order of the Rising Sun|Grand Cordon of the Order of the Rising Sun with Paulownia Flowers]] (April 1). (Second Class: August 20, 1895; Third Class: April 7, 1885) * 1905: [[:en:Pour le Mérite|Pour le Mérite]] (January 10) * 1907: Grand Cross of the [[:en:Legion of Honour|Legion of Honour]] (April 16) * 1909: Chilean Gold Medal of Merit (April 28) * 1911: Grand Cross of the Order of the Star of Romania (October 25) * 1911: Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the [[Royal Victorian Order|Knights Grand Cross of the Royal Victorian Order]] (GCVO) * 1911: Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the [[:en:Order of the Bath|Order of the Bath]], Military Division (UK) (GCB) (January 1).[http://www.london-gazette.co.uk/about London Gazette:] [http://www.london-gazette.co.uk/issues/28567/supplements/1 Issue No. 28567, p. 1 (29 December 1911).] ===Court order of precedence=== * 1871: Senior seventh Rank (December) * 1873: Sixth Rank (June 25) * 1879: Senior sixth Rank (December 20) * 1880: Fifth Rank (June 8) * 1885: Senior fifth Rank (July 25) * 1893: Senior fourth Rank (April 11) * 1896: Third Rank (December 21) * 1904: Senior third Rank (June 6) * 1909: Second Rank (July 10) * 1916: Senior second Rank (posthumous) ==Portrayals== Maresuke was portrayed by [[Tatsuya Nakadai]] in the 1980 Japanese [[:en:War film|war]] [[:en:Drama (film and television)|drama film]] ''[[The Battle of Port Arthur]]'' (sometimes referred as ''203 Kochi'').[https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0080316/ ''The Battle of Port Arthur'' (''203 Koshi'')] in the [[:en:Internet Movie Database|Internet Movie Database]] Directed by [[Toshio Masuda (director)|Toshio Masuda]] the film depicted the [[Siege of Port Arthur]] during the [[Russo-Japanese War]] and starred Nakadai as General Maresuke, [[Tetsurō Tamba]] as General [[:en:Kodama Gentarō|Kodama Gentarō]], and [[Toshiro Mifune|Toshirō Mifune]] as [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]. In the [[:en:NHK|NHK]] television adaptation of [[Ryōtarō Shiba]]'s epic [[:en:Saka no Ue no Kumo (TV series)|''Saka no Ue no Kumo'']], which aired from 2009 to 2011, Nogi was portrayed by actor [[:en:Akira Emoto|Akira Emoto]]. In the manga and [[:en:NHK|NHK]] television adaptation of ''[[:en:Monster (manga)|Monster]]'', General Nogi is mentioned by the Turkish elder and community leader, Mr. Deniz, convincing the others to trust Dr. Kenzo Tenma and a local prostitute when they attempt to convince the leaders of FRankfurt's Turkish Quarter to be wary of an imminent arson attack by neo-Nazis, led by The Baby. Deniz makes reference to an incident wherein General Nogi saved an Ottoman fleet of the Turkish Navy that had run aground in the Pacific. Although this is most likely a confusion with [[:en:Yamada Torajirō|Yamada Torajirō]] who did assist after the sinking of [[:en:Ottoman frigate Ertuğrul#Shipwreck|Ottoman frigate Ertuğrul#Shipwreck]]. == Notes == {{reflist}} == References == {{refbegin}} * [[:en:Herbert Bix|Bix]], Herbert P. {{short description|Japanese general (1849–1912)}} {{about|the general|other uses|Nogi (disambiguation)}} {{family name hatnote|Nogi|lang=Japanese}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2020}} {{Infobox officeholder | honorific_prefix = [[Kazoku|Count]] | name = Nogi Maresuke | image = Maresuke Nogi 2.jpg | image_size = | caption = Nogi standing before his house in Nogizaka, Tokyo, shortly before his suicide in 1912 | office = [[:en:Governor-General of Taiwan|Governor General of Taiwan]] | monarch = Meiji | term_start = 14 October 1896 | term_end = 26 February 1898 | predecessor = [[:en:Katsura Tarō|Katsura Tarō]] | successor = [[:en:Kodama Gentarō|Kodama Gentarō]] | nickname = Kiten
Count Nogi | birth_date = {{Birth date|1849|12|25}} | birth_place = [[:en:Edo, Japan|Edo, Japan]] | death_date = {{Death date and age|1912|09|13|1849|12|25}} | death_place = [[Tokyo]], Japan | placeofburial = | allegiance = {{flag|Empire of Japan}} | branch = {{army|Empire of Japan}} | serviceyears = 1871–1908 | Rank = [[File:帝國陸軍の階級―肩章―大将.svg|50px]] [[Four-star Rank|General]] | unit = | commands = | battles = {{tree list}} * [[Satsuma Rebellion]] * [[:en:First Sino-Japanese War|First Sino-Japanese War]] * [[Russo-Japanese War]] ** [[Siege of Port Arthur]] {{tree list/end}} | awards = {{Plainlist| * Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Rising Sun|Order of the Rising Sun]] with Paulownia Flowers * Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Golden Kite|Order of the Golden Kite]] * Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Sacred Treasure|Order of the Sacred Treasure]] * Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the [[:en:Order of the Bath|Order of the Bath]] (UK) * Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the [[Royal Victorian Order]] (UK)}} | relations = | laterwork = | native_name = {{nobold|乃木 希典}} | native_name_lang = ja | honorific_suffix = [[Senior Second Rank]] }} [[:en:Count|Count]] {{nihongo|'''Nogi Maresuke''' |乃木 希典|}}, also known as '''Kiten, Count Nogi''' [[:en:Grand Cross of the Order of the Bath|GCB]] (December 25, 1849{{spnd}}September 13, 1912), was a Japanese [[:en:General|General]] in the [[:en:Imperial Japanese Army|Imperial Japanese Army]] and a [[:en:Governor-General of Taiwan|governor-general of Taiwan]]. He was one of the commanders during the [[:en:Battle of Lushunkou|1894 capture of Port Arthur from China]] and a prominent figure in the [[Russo-Japanese War]] of 1904–05, as commander of the forces [[Siege of Port Arthur|which captured Port Arthur]] from the Russians. He was a national hero in Imperial Japan as a model of feudal loyalty and self-sacrifice, ultimately to the point of suicide. In the [[Satsuma Rebellion]], he lost a banner of the emperor in battle, for which he tried to atone with suicidal bravery in order to recapture it, until ordered to stop. In the [[Russo-Japanese War]], he captured Port Arthur but he felt that he had lost too many of his soldiers, so requested permission to commit suicide, which the emperor refused. These two events, as well as his desire not to outlive his master, motivated his suicide on the day of the funeral of the [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]. His example brought attention to the concept of ''[[:en:Bushido|Bushido]]'' and the controversial samurai practice of ''[[:en:Junshi|Junshi]]'' (following the lord in death).[[Oleg Benesch|Benesch, Oleg]]. (2014). ''Inventing the Way of the Samurai'', p. 153. == Early life == '''Nogi Nakito''' was born on December 25, 1849, at the [[:en:Chofu Domain|Chōfu Domain]] Mansion in [[:en:Edo|Edo]] (present-day [[Roppongi]], [[Tokyo]]), the third son of [[samurai]] cavalry officer (''umamawari'') Nogi Maretsugu and his wife Hisako. His father served the [[:en:Chofu Domain|Chōfu Domain]], a subsidiary domain of the [[:en:Chōshū Domain|Chōshū Domain]], and held land worth 80 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]''. His childhood name was Nakito (無人),{{Cite book |last=Ōhama |first=Tetsuya |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/744210173 |title=Nogi maresuke |date=2010 |publisher=Kōdansha |isbn=978-4-06-292028-5 |pages=19 |oclc=744210173}} literally "no one", to prevent evil spirits from coming to harm him. He was briefly known as Bunzō, after which he was renamed Maresuke. As he claimed descent from the [[:en:Izumo Province|Izumo]] [[Minamoto clan]] through the [[Sasaki clan]], he often used the name Minamoto no Maresuke in his signatures.{{Cite book |last1=Sasaki |first1=Hideaki |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/61402590 |title=Nogi Maresuke : yo wa shokun no shitei o koroshitari |last2=佐々木英昭 |date=2005 |publisher=Mineruva Shobō |isbn=4-623-04406-8 |edition=Shohan |pages=40, 113 |oclc=61402590}} == Early military career == In November 1869, by the order of the [[Nagato province|Nagato]] domain's lord, he enlisted in ''Fushimi Goshin Heisha'' ({{literal|the Fushimi Loyal Guard Barrack}}) to be trained in the French style for the domanial Army. After completing the training, he was reassigned to the Kawatō Barrack in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] as an instructor, and then as Toyōra domain's Army trainer in charge of coastal defense troops. In 1871, Nogi was commissioned as a [[Major (Rank)|major]] in the fledgling [[:en:Imperial Japanese Army|Imperial Japanese Army]]. Around this time, he renamed himself ''Maresuke'' taking a ''[[:en:Kanji|Kanji]]'' from the name of his father. In 1875, he became the 14th Infantry Regiment's attaché. The next year (1876), Nogi was named as the [[:en:Kumamoto|Kumamoto]] regional troop's Staff Officer, and transferred to command the 1st Infantry Regiment, and for his service in the [[Satsuma Rebellion]], against the forces of [[Saigō Takamori]] in [[Kyushu|Kyūshū]], he was promoted to [[:en:lieutenant colonel|lieutenant colonel]] on April 22, 1877. In a fierce battle at that time, he lost the 14th Infantry Regiment's regimental banner, which was considered to be the property of the Emperor, to the enemy. Its loss was an extreme disgrace. Nogi considered this such a grave mistake that he listed it as one of the reasons for his later suicide.Bix, Herbert. (2000). ''Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan,'' p. 42. On August 27, 1876, Nogi married Shizuko, the fourth daughter of [[Satsuma han|Satsuma]] ''samurai'' Yuji Sadano, who was then 20 years old. As Nogi was 28 years old, it was a very late marriage for that time, considering that the average age to marry was in the early 20s. On August 28, 1877, their first son Katsunori was born, and Nogi bought his first house at Niizakamachi, [[:en:Akasaka, Tokyo|Akasaka, Tokyo]]. In 1879, his second son Yasunori was born.{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}} He was promoted to [[:en:Colonel|Colonel]] on April 29, 1880. He was posted to Nagoya during the early Meiji era. The warehouse in the Sannomaru enceinte of [[Nagoya Castle]] was probably constructed in 1880 (Meiji 13) as an army ammunition depot. It was named later after him.{{cite web | url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/113094 | title=乃木倉庫 文化遺産オンライン }} Promoted [[:en:major general|major general]] on May 21, 1885, in 1887 Nogi went to [[:en:Germany|Germany]] with [[:en:Kawakami Soroku|Kawakami Soroku]] to study European [[:en:Military strategy|Military strategy]] and tactics.National Diet Library: "Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures," [http://www.ndl.go.jp/portrait/e/datas/160.html?c=7 Nogi Maresuke.] In 1894, during the [[:en:First Sino-Japanese War|First Sino-Japanese War]], Major-General Nogi commanded the First Infantry Brigade which penetrated the Chinese defenses and successfully occupied [[:en:Lüshunkou|Port Arthur]] in only one day of combat. As such, he was a senior commander during the [[:en:Port Arthur massacre (China)|Port Arthur massacre]]. The following year, he was promoted to [[:en:lieutenant general|lieutenant general]] (April 29, 1895) and assigned to the [[:en:2nd Division (Imperial Japanese Army)|Second Division]], tasked with the [[:en:Japanese invasion of Taiwan (1895)|invasion of Taiwan]]. Nogi remained with the occupation forces in Taiwan until 1898. In 1899, he was recalled to Japan, and placed in command of the newly formed 11th Infantry Brigade, based in [[:en:Kagawa Prefecture|Kagawa]].{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}}{{Cite book|title=500 Great Military Leaders|last=Tucker|first=Spencer C.|publisher=ABC-CLIO|date=December 16, 2014|isbn=978-1598847574|pages=560}} == Political career == After the war, he was elevated to ''danshaku'' ([[:en:Baron|Baron]]); and he was conferred with the [[:en:Order of the Golden Kite|Order of the Golden Kite]], 1st class.[https://books.google.com/books?id=x70UAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA1139&dq= "Nogi, Maresuke,"] ''Encyclopædia Britannica'' (12th ed.), Vol. XXX, p. 1139. Nogi was appointed as the third Japanese [[:en:Governor-General of Taiwan|Governor-General of Taiwan]] from October 14, 1896, to February 1898. When moving to Taiwan, he moved his entire family, and during their time in Taiwan, his mother contracted [[:en:Malaria|Malaria]] and died. This led Nogi to take measures to improve on the health care infrastructure of the island. However, unlike many of his contemporaries as officers, Nogi expressed no interest in pursuing politics.{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}} == Russo-Japanese War == [[File:Fronte (15).jpg|thumb|right|Nogi standing in the center facing a captured Russian gun crew outside [[:en:Port Arthur naval base|Port Arthur]] on January 2, 1905]] In 1904, Nogi was recalled to active service on the occasion of the [[Russo-Japanese War]], and was promoted to army [[:en:General|General]] in command of the [[:en:Japanese Third Army|Japanese Third Army]], with an initial strength of approximately 90,000 men and assigned to the capture of the [[Russia]]n-held [[:en:Lüshunkou|Port Arthur]] on the southern tip of [[:en:en:Liaodong Peninsula|en:Liaodong Peninsula]], [[:en:Manchuria|Manchuria]]. Nogi's forces landed shortly after the [[:en:Battle of Nanshan|Battle of Nanshan]], in which his eldest son, serving with the [[:en:Japanese Second Army|Japanese Second Army]], was killed.Connaughton, Richard. (1988). ''Rising Sun and Tumbling Bear'', p. 101. Advancing slowly down the Liaodong Peninsula, Nogi encountered unexpectedly strong resistance, and far more fortifications than he had experienced ten years earlier against the Chinese. [[Image:Nogi and Stessel.jpg|thumb|left|Nogi is seated in the center next to Russian general [[:en:Anatoly Stessel|Anatoly Stessel]] after Russian forces surrendered at Port Arthur on January 2, 1905.]] The attack against Port Arthur quickly turned into the lengthy [[Siege of Port Arthur]], an engagement lasting from August 1, 1904, to January 2, 1905, costing the Japanese massive losses. Due to the mounting casualties and failure of Nogi to overcome Port Arthur's defenses, there was mounting pressure within the Japanese government and military to relieve him of command. However, in an unprecedented action, [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] spoke out during the [[Supreme War Council (Japan)]] meeting, defending Nogi and demanding that he be kept in command.{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}} After the fall of Port Arthur, Nogi was regarded as a national hero. He led his Third Army against the Russian forces at the final [[:en:Battle of Mukden|Battle of Mukden]], ending the land combat phase of operations of the war.Jukes, Geoffrey. (2002). ''The Russo-Japanese War 1904–1905'', p. 66. British historian [[Richard Storry]] noted that Nogi imposed the best of the Japanese ''samurai'' tradition on the men under his command such that "...the conduct of the Japanese during the Russo-Japanese War towards both prisoners and Chinese civilians won the respect, and indeed admiration, of the world".[[Richard Storry|Storry, Richard]]. (1960). ''A History of Modern Japan'', p. 217. Both of Nogi's sons, who were army lieutenants during the war, were killed in action. Though Nogi's elder son Katsunori (August 28, 1879 – May 27, 1904) had been a sickly child, he had managed to enter the imperial military academy on his third try. He was hit in the abdomen at the Battle of Nanshan and died of blood loss while undergoing surgery at a field hospital. His second son Yasunori (December 16, 1881 – November 30, 1904), a second lieutenant at Port Arthur, fell on a rocky slope, striking his head and dying instantly. Yasunori received a posthumous promotion to lieutenant, and was buried by his father in the Aoyama cemetery. At the end of the war, Nogi made a report directly to Emperor Meiji during a ''[[:en:Gozen Kaigi|Gozen Kaigi]]''. When explaining battles of the Siege of Port Arthur in detail, he broke down and wept, apologizing for the 56,000 lives lost in that campaign and asking to be allowed to kill himself in atonement. Emperor Meiji told him that suicide was unacceptable, as all responsibility for the war was due to imperial orders, and that Nogi must remain alive, at least as long as he himself lived.Keene, Donald. (2005). '' Emperor of Japan, Meiji and his World'', pp. 712–713. == Postwar career == After the war, Nogi was elevated to the title of [[:en:Count|Count]] and awarded the [[:en:Order of the Rising Sun|Order of the Rising Sun with Paulownia Flowers, Grand Cordon]], 1907. As head of the [[:en:Gakushuin|Peers' School]] from 1908 to 1912, he was the mentor of the young [[:en:Hirohito|Hirohito]], and was, perhaps, the most important influence on the life of the future emperor of Japan.Bix, Herbert. (2000). ''Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan,'' pp. 36-37, 43. Nogi spent most of his personal fortune on hospitals for wounded soldiers and on memorial monuments erected around the country in commemoration of those killed during the Russo-Japanese War. He also successfully petitioned the Japanese government to erect a Russian-style memorial monument in Port Arthur to the Russian dead of that campaign.{{Citation needed|date=September 2007}} == Scouting == Nogi is significant to [[Scout Association of Japan|Scouting in Japan]], as in 1911, he went to England in attendance on [[:en:Prince Higashifushimi Yorihito|Prince Higashifushimi Yorihito]] for the [[:en:Coronation of George V and Mary|coronation of King George V]]. The General, as the "Defender of Port Arthur" was introduced to [[Robert Baden-Powell, 1st Baron Baden-Powell|General Robert Baden-Powell]], the "Defender of [[Siege of Mafeking|Mafeking]]", by [[:en:Herbert Kitchener, 1st Earl Kitchener|Lord Kitchener]], whose expression "Once a Scout, always a Scout" remains to this day. == Suicide == [[File:Room in which Nogi committed suicide with his wife.JPG|thumb|upright|Room in which Nogi Maresuke committed suicide with his wife]] Nogi and his wife Shizuko committed suicide by ''[[seppuku]]'' shortly after the [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]'s funeral cortege left the palace.Noss, John Boyer. (1980). ''Man's Religions'', p. 319. The ritual suicide was in accordance with the ''samurai'' practice of following one's master to death (''[[:en:Junshi|Junshi]]'').Lyell, Thomas. (1948). ''Case History of Japan,'' p. 142. In his [[suicide letter]], he said that he wished to expiate for his disgrace in Kyūshū, and for the thousands of casualties at Port Arthur. He also donated his body to medical science.[[Image:House of Maresuke Nogi.jpg|thumb|left|House of Maresuke Nogi in [[Nogizaka]]]]All four members of the Nogi family are buried at [[:en:Aoyama Cemetery|Aoyama Cemetery]] in Tokyo. Under [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], Nogi was revered as a ''[[kami]]''. [[Nogi Shrine (Tokyo)|Nogi Shrine]], a [[Shinto shrine]] in his honor, still exists on the site of his house in [[:en:Minato, Tokyo|Nogizaka]], Tokyo. His memory is also honored in other locations such as the [[Nogi Shrine (Kyoto)|Nogi Shrine]] in [[Fushimi-ku, Kyoto#Sights|Fushimi-ku]], Kyoto, where the mausoleum of Emperor Meiji was established.[http://www.geocities.jp/kyo_nogi/ Nogi Jinja] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121022151620/http://www.geocities.jp/kyo_nogi/ |date=October 22, 2012 }}, Kyoto. == Legacy == [[File:Nogi-jinja (Minato, Tokyo).jpg|thumb|Nogi Shrine in Nogizaka]] [[Image:Ziziphus jujuba.jpg|thumb|right|150px|The [[Ziziphus jujuba]] which written in ''[[:en:Monbusho|Monbusho]]'' chant lyrics, located in Nogi's mansion]] Nogi's ''seppuku'' immediately created a sensation and a controversy. Some writers claimed that it reflected Nogi's disgust with the profligacy and decline in moral values of late Meiji Japan. Others pointed to Nogi's own suicide note, calling it an act of atonement for mistakes in his military career. In either case, Nogi's suicide marked the end of an era, and it had a profound impact on contemporary writers, such as [[:en:Mori Ōgai|Mori Ōgai]], [[:en:Kuroiwa Shūroku|Kuroiwa Ruikō]] and [[:en:Natsume Sōseki|Natsume Sōseki]]. For the public, Nogi became a symbol of loyalty and sacrifice. The epic historical novel ''[[:en:Saka no Ue no Kumo|Saka no Ue no Kumo]]'' portrays Nogi as floundering at the [[Siege of Port Arthur]] and having to be relieved by [[:en:Kodama Gentarō|Kodama Gentarō]]. Several books have been released in recent years rehabilitating Nogi's image and showing he was a competent leader. [[File:Nagoya cstl nogi soko.jpg|thumb|left|Nogi Warehouse at [[Nagoya Castle]]]] The Nogi Warehouse in the Sannomaru enceinte of Nagoya Castle was named after him.{{cite web | url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/113094 | title=乃木倉庫 文化遺産オンライン }} ==Man of letters== Nogi is also noted in Japan as a man of letters. His [[:en:Kanshi (poetry)|Kanshi]] poems ([[:en:Chinese poetry|poems in the Chinese language]]) were especially popular among the Japanese during his time. Three of his Kanshi poems are famous.[http://www.nogijinja.or.jp/shahou/main.html Gen. Nogi's Relics at Nogi Shrine] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120225022226/http://www.nogijinja.or.jp/shahou/main.html |date=February 25, 2012 }} (in Japanese) Right after the [[:en:Battle of Nanshan|Battle of Nanshan]] of 1904, in which he lost his eldest son, he wrote: {| class="wikitable" style="margin:auto" |- !　金州城外の作 ! Written Outside the Walls of [[:en:Jinzhou District|Jinzhou]] |- | align=left | 山川草木轉荒涼
十里風腥新戰場
征馬不前人不語
金州城外立斜陽 | align=left | Mountains and rivers, trees and grass, have become cold and desolate.
For ten ''[[:en:Li (unit)|li]]'', the foul odor of blood drifts on the wind over new battlefields.
My brave horse would not advance, and the soldiers are silent.
I stand outside Jinzhou Town, in the setting sun. |} After the battle of [[:en:Hill 203|Hill 203]] of 1904–05, in which he lost his second son, he wrote: {| class="wikitable" style="margin:auto" |- ! 爾靈山 ! Nireisan |- | align=left | 爾靈山嶮豈難攀
男子功名期克艱
鐵血覆山山形改
萬人齊仰爾靈山 | align=left | Nireisan was indeed difficult to climb,
But it was overcome by the deeds of young men.
Under a mantle of iron and blood, the mountain's shape is changed.
Now all look up in awe at Nireisan. |} After the end of the [[Russo-Japanese War]], he wrote: {| class="wikitable" style="margin:auto" |- ! 凱旋 ! Triumphant Return |- | align=left | 皇師百萬征強虜
野戰攻城屍作山
愧我何顔看父老
凱歌今日幾人還 | align=left | The Emperor's army, a million strong, set out to punish the powerful savages of the north.
On the battlefield, in the midst of the sieges, the bodies of the dead piled up like mountains.
I am ashamed to show my face to the fathers who remain back home,
though we few return today in triumph. |} == Honors == [[Image:Maresuke Nogi stamp.jpg|thumb|145px|An [[:en:Empire of Japan|Imperial Japanese]] stamp from 1938 depicting Nogi]] ===Peerages=== * 1895: Baron (August 20) * 1907: Count (September 21) ===Decorations=== * 1897: Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Sacred Treasure|Order of the Sacred Treasure]] (June 26; Second Class: April 29, 1894) * 1906: Grand Cordon of the [[:en:Order of the Golden Kite|Order of the Golden Kite]] (April 1) (Third Class: August 20, 1895) * 1906: [[:en:Order of the Rising Sun|Grand Cordon of the Order of the Rising Sun with Paulownia Flowers]] (April 1). (Second Class: August 20, 1895; Third Class: April 7, 1885) * 1905: [[:en:Pour le Mérite|Pour le Mérite]] (January 10) * 1907: Grand Cross of the [[:en:Legion of Honour|Legion of Honour]] (April 16) * 1909: Chilean Gold Medal of Merit (April 28) * 1911: Grand Cross of the Order of the Star of Romania (October 25) * 1911: Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the [[Royal Victorian Order|Knights Grand Cross of the Royal Victorian Order]] (GCVO) * 1911: Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the [[:en:Order of the Bath|Order of the Bath]], Military Division (UK) (GCB) (January 1).[http://www.london-gazette.co.uk/about London Gazette:] [http://www.london-gazette.co.uk/issues/28567/supplements/1 Issue No. 28567, p. 1 (29 December 1911).] ===Court order of precedence=== * 1871: Senior seventh Rank (December) * 1873: Sixth Rank (June 25) * 1879: Senior sixth Rank (December 20) * 1880: Fifth Rank (June 8) * 1885: Senior fifth Rank (July 25) * 1893: Senior fourth Rank (April 11) * 1896: Third Rank (December 21) * 1904: Senior third Rank (June 6) * 1909: Second Rank (July 10) * 1916: Senior second Rank (posthumous) ==Portrayals== Maresuke was portrayed by [[Tatsuya Nakadai]] in the 1980 Japanese [[:en:War film|war]] [[:en:Drama (film and television)|drama film]] ''[[The Battle of Port Arthur]]'' (sometimes referred as ''203 Kochi'').[https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0080316/ ''The Battle of Port Arthur'' (''203 Koshi'')] in the [[:en:Internet Movie Database|Internet Movie Database]] Directed by [[Toshio Masuda (director)|Toshio Masuda]] the film depicted the [[Siege of Port Arthur]] during the [[Russo-Japanese War]] and starred Nakadai as General Maresuke, [[Tetsurō Tamba]] as General [[:en:Kodama Gentarō|Kodama Gentarō]], and [[Toshiro Mifune|Toshirō Mifune]] as [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]. In the [[:en:NHK|NHK]] television adaptation of [[Ryōtarō Shiba]]'s epic [[:en:Saka no Ue no Kumo (TV series)|''Saka no Ue no Kumo'']], which aired from 2009 to 2011, Nogi was portrayed by actor [[:en:Akira Emoto|Akira Emoto]]. In the manga and [[:en:NHK|NHK]] television adaptation of ''[[:en:Monster (manga)|Monster]]'', General Nogi is mentioned by the Turkish elder and community leader, Mr. Deniz, convincing the others to trust Dr. Kenzo Tenma and a local prostitute when they attempt to convince the leaders of FRankfurt's Turkish Quarter to be wary of an imminent arson attack by neo-Nazis, led by The Baby. Deniz makes reference to an incident wherein General Nogi saved an Ottoman fleet of the Turkish Navy that had run aground in the Pacific. Although this is most likely a confusion with [[:en:Yamada Torajirō|Yamada Torajirō]] who did assist after the sinking of [[:en:Ottoman frigate Ertuğrul#Shipwreck|Ottoman frigate Ertuğrul#Shipwreck]]. == Notes == {{reflist}} == References == {{refbegin}} * [[:en:Herbert Bix|Bix]], Herbert P.
